presentingComplaint: Reduced urine output and increasing lethargy for 3 days
history: Type 2 diabetic for 18 years and hypertensive with known stage 3b CKD (baseline creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, eGFR ~38 six weeks ago). Presented after a 4-day diarrhoeal-vomiting illness during which he continued his usual ramipril and indapamide and self-medicated with diclofenac for backache. Family report he has passed only small volumes of concentrated urine for 3 days despite drinking little. Over the last 24h he has become drowsy, nauseated and off his food, with generalised itch and a metallic taste. No fever, no rash, no dysuria, no flank pain, no haematuria and no recent contrast imaging. This acute deterioration on a background of pre-existing CKD and diabetes is the source of diagnostic confounding - the question is how much is new (acute) versus chronic.
examination: Elderly man, drowsy but rousable, looks dry: reduced skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3s, empty neck veins on inspection. No peripheral or sacral oedema. Chest clear, no added heart sounds. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no palpable bladder, no bruit, kidneys not ballotable. Uraemic flap (asterixis) present. No focal neurology, no meningism. Fundi show background diabetic retinopathy.

labs.urinalysis: trace protein, no blood, no leucocytes/nitrites; occasional hyaline and muddy-brown granular casts

imaging: Renal ultrasound: both kidneys normal in position, mildly echogenic (chronic change), right 9.6 cm and left 9.9 cm, no hydronephrosis, no stones, no post-void residual - obstruction excluded, kidney size preserved rather than shrunken suggesting largely reversible acute component.
microbiology: Not applicable - no clinical evidence of infection; blood and urine cultures sent for completeness and were negative at 48h.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute kidney injury (acute-on-chronic; prerenal/ischaemic ATN from volume depletion, ACE-inhibitor, diuretic and NSAID - 'triple whammy')
Progression of underlying diabetic CKD alone
finalDiagnosis: Acute kidney injury (KDIGO stage 3, acute-on-chronic) - prerenal azotaemia progressing to ischaemic acute tubular necrosis, precipitated by GI fluid losses plus RAAS blockade, diuretic and NSAID nephrotoxicity, on a background of diabetic CKD stage 3b, complicated by hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis.
citations: KDIGO - Acute Kidney Injury Clinical Practice Guideline - 2012
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Acute Kidney Injury
stewardship: Not applicable - this is a non-infective presentation. No antibiotics indicated. Stewardship focus is on nephrotoxin stewardship: stop the ACE-inhibitor, diuretic and NSAID, avoid contrast and other nephrotoxins, and renally dose all drugs.
contraindications: Do NOT continue ramipril, indapamide or diclofenac in acute volume depletion with rising creatinine (the nephrotoxic 'triple whammy')
Avoid iodinated contrast and nephrotoxic antibiotics (e.g., aminoglycosides) unless unavoidable
Avoid potassium-containing fluids and hold metformin (lactic-acidosis risk with eGFR <30) and SGLT2 inhibitors during acute illness
Do not give large potassium-sparing or Hartmann's boluses given K+ 6.2
edgeCases: Distinguishing acute-on-chronic AKI from stable CKD: preserved kidney size, near-normal recent baseline and muddy-brown casts favour a reversible acute component
Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes may be the immediate life threat and dictates emergency treatment before the AKI workup is complete
If oliguria and acidosis fail to respond to volume resuscitation and hyperkalaemia is refractory, urgent dialysis is indicated (AEIOU criteria)
Diabetes and CKD can mask or mimic features - euvolaemia may be misjudged, and HHS/DKA must be excluded as an alternative cause of the metabolic disturbance
expectedMaiK: Acute-on-chronic AKI (KDIGO stage 3) from prerenal/ischaemic ATN due to volume depletion plus ACEi/diuretic/NSAID nephrotoxicity in a diabetic with CKD; priorities are treating hyperkalaemia, isotonic volume resuscitation, and stopping all nephrotoxins.
expectedNextQuestions: What is the patient's baseline creatinine/eGFR and how fast has it changed?
Full drug history including ACE-inhibitors/ARBs, diuretics, NSAIDs, metformin and any recent contrast?
Quantify fluid losses and urine output - is he anuric/oliguric?
Any features of obstruction, glomerulonephritis (haematuria, oedema) or systemic disease?
expectedInvestigations: Serum creatinine, urea and electrolytes with potassium (compare to baseline)
Venous blood gas / bicarbonate for metabolic acidosis
12-lead ECG to look for hyperkalaemic changes
Urinalysis with microscopy (casts) and urine electrolytes / FeNa
Renal tract ultrasound to exclude obstruction and assess kidney size

investigations: Serum creatinine and urea versus baseline

regressionAssertions: Engine must return aki as the top diagnosis given oliguria, dehydration, acute rise in creatinine/urea over a CKD baseline, and nephrotoxin exposure
Must not recommend antibiotics for this non-infective presentation
Must flag hyperkalaemia (K+ 6.2) and metabolic acidosis as urgent complications requiring treatment
Must advise stopping ACE-inhibitor, diuretic and NSAID and avoiding further nephrotoxins
Must not misclassify as stable CKD alone given the acute change from baseline and preserved kidney size on ultrasound
